item.title: 1Password SSH Agent and CLI: Read-Only AI Agent Access
item.description: Design a read-only SSH workflow with 1Password CLI, the SSH Agent, and MCP. Use synthetic commands, narrow permissions, and human approval before live testing.
item.content:encoded:
Read the full article at https://simeononsecurity.com/

A command-line agent needs useful access, not a copy of every credential. This guide presents a bounded design for 1Password CLI, the 1Password SSH Agent, Bitbucket Git access, and Model Context Protocol (MCP). The first workflow uses synthetic names, read-only actions, and human approval at the SSH boundary.

The key distinction is simple. Interactive SSH uses consent through the 1Password SSH Agent. Unattended automation needs a separate identity, narrow access, and a different key lifecycle. Do not treat an MCP connection as permission to run either workflow.

Key Takeaways #

  • Private-key protection: The 1Password SSH Agent performs SSH authentication while keeping private keys inside the 1Password app.
  • Public-key handling: Publish only a public key to Bitbucket or a remote account. Keep the private half in an SSH Key item.
  • Interactive consent: A person approves a client or terminal session before the SSH Agent uses a key.
  • Unattended separation: A scheduled job needs a dedicated service account and a narrow vault scope. An interactive SSH Agent approval does not satisfy this need.
  • MCP boundaries: MCP connects an agent to tools and resources. The client, server, operating system, and 1Password policy still control access.

Before You Begin #

Prerequisites: Install 1Password 8 and 1Password CLI 2.20.0 or later. Sign in through a supported 1Password account. Use an OpenSSH client. Create a test Bitbucket repository or another non-production target. Keep a second administrative path available for rollback.

Time: 30 to 45 minutes for a design review and synthetic walkthrough.

Difficulty: Intermediate. You need basic Git, SSH, shell, and access-control knowledge.

This guide covers design and planning. The linked Bitbucket article covers Bitbucket-specific access boundaries. This guide does not test a live account, create a real key, connect to a real h

item.title: Bitbucket Cloud SSH Keys: Read-Only Git Access for AI Agents
item.description: Set up Bitbucket Cloud SSH keys, Git CLI access, REST API tokens, 1Password, and MCP tools for read-only AI agent workflows.
item.content:encoded:
Read the full article at https://simeononsecurity.com/

A bounded agent workflow separates repository reads, API reads, secret handling, and remote writes. Use Git over Secure Shell (SSH) for source access, a read-only Bitbucket access key for automated checkout, the REST API for metadata, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for approved tools. Store private keys and API tokens in 1Password. Keep writes behind a human approval step.

Key Takeaways #

  • Read-only default: Use a repository or project access key for agent checkout. Neither grants push access.
  • Personal identity: Use a personal SSH key for interactive work tied to a user account.
  • Secret custody: Use the 1Password SSH Agent so Git receives a signing operation without reading the private key.
  • CLI meaning: Treat git, curl, and a small audited API wrapper as the practical Bitbucket command line.
  • MCP boundary: Expose narrow read tools. Keep write tools disabled or behind a separate approval path.
  • Write gate: Let an agent inspect, compare, and prepare a change. Require a human to approve a push, pull request, merge, or settings update.

Before You Begin #

Prerequisites: Bitbucket Cloud access, Git, an OpenSSH client, 1Password 8, 1Password CLI, a signed-in CLI or approved service account, and an MCP host with server approval controls. Set aside 45 minutes. Difficulty is intermediate.

Use a test repository for the first pass. Replace every placeholder in the examples. The commands below are untested examples. They do not represent a live Bitbucket account or repository.

item.title: Migrate a Hyper-V VM to Proxmox VE: A Reversible Checklist
item.description: Move one Hyper-V virtual machine to Proxmox VE with a stopped-source export, matched firmware, disk import, isolated boot test, and rollback plan.
item.content:encoded:
Read the full article at https://simeononsecurity.com/

A Hyper-V export preserves a virtual machine’s files, while Proxmox VE needs a new guest configuration and imported VHDX virtual disk files. A successful copy alone does not prove the guest will boot or serve users. This checklist moves one VM through a stopped-source export, a controlled boot test, and a cutover with a clear return path.

Key Takeaways #

  • Record the source: Capture firmware generation, disk paths, checkpoints, network settings, and encryption before export.
  • Stop writes: Shut down the Hyper-V VM before the final export and keep it off during the Proxmox test.
  • Match the boot path: Hyper-V Generation 1 uses legacy BIOS. Generation 2 uses UEFI.
  • Validate the service: Check data, network access, backups, and guest health before retiring the source.

Before You Begin #

Plan a maintenance window and a test on a disposable VM first. You need administrator access to Hyper-V, Proxmox VE, storage for the export, and a verified backup separate from the migration copy. Allow time to transfer every virtual disk and test the guest application. Disk size and transfer speed set the downtime.

This procedure covers a conventional VM with virtual disks. Shielded VMs, pass-through disks, shared disks, clustered workloads, and hardware-bound licensing need workload-specific plans. Record who owns the cutover decision and the latest time you will roll back. Do not start both copies on the production network with the same machine identity.

Read More at https://simeononsecurity.com/
Source detail Why you need it
VM generation and firmware Select SeaBIOS or OVMF on Proxmox
Secure Boot state and template Match the boot policy and enroll compatible keys
Boot and data disks Import every required VHDX virtual disk file in the right order

item.title: Proxmox VM Backup Restore Drill: Prove the Guest Works
item.description: Test a Proxmox VM backup with an isolated restore. Check disk coverage, backup mode, guest data, service health, and recovery time without touching production.
item.content:encoded:
Read the full article at https://simeononsecurity.com/

A green backup task tells you Proxmox wrote a backup. The task does not show whether the guest boots, its data is recent, or its main service works. Restore a copy under a new VM ID on an isolated network. The result gives you evidence for recovery before an outage forces the test.

This drill covers one Proxmox VE virtual machine. Containers have different backup rules, especially for bind and device mounts. The site’s homelab backup restore drill covers broader file recovery. Here, you will test a Proxmox VM backup and its workload.

A guest is the operating system running inside a virtual machine. Bind mounts and device mounts expose host resources to a guest. Test those resources through a separate recovery plan.

Key Takeaways #

  • Define success first: Name a data item, a service check, and an acceptable recovery time.
  • Inspect coverage: A VM backup skips disks marked No backup and cannot recreate external services or omitted data.
  • Restore separately: Use an unused VM ID and keep the restored network isolated from production.
  • Record evidence: Measure backup age, restore time, boot, disk presence, and a real application check.

item.title: Test Browser DNS and WebRTC Leaks With a VPN
item.description: Check your browser's public IP, DNS resolver, and WebRTC addresses before and after connecting a VPN. Interpret results and isolate routing problems.
item.content:encoded:
Read the full article at https://simeononsecurity.com/

A virtual private network (VPN) connection icon does not prove every browser request follows the same route. Test your public IP, Domain Name System (DNS) resolver, and WebRTC addresses separately. Each result answers a different question. This guide gives you a repeatable check and a way to investigate an unexpected result.

Key Takeaways #

  • Compare two states: Record the same tests before and after connecting your VPN.
  • Read each result separately: A changed public IP does not establish where DNS queries went.
  • Check WebRTC candidates: Look for a public address from outside your intended route. A private address has a different meaning.
  • Change one setting: Retest after each VPN, browser, or DNS adjustment.

Before You Begin #

Use the browser and network connection you intend to protect. Know whether your VPN should cover the whole device or only selected apps. If your VPN uses split tunneling, record whether the test browser belongs inside the tunnel. Keep the VPN client’s DNS policy available for comparison.

Split tunneling sends selected apps through the VPN while other apps use the normal network.

item.title: Test Guest and IoT Isolation on a Mesh Wi-Fi Network
item.description: Verify whether your mesh guest and IoT networks block access to your home devices. Use a known working service, test each network, and record the limits.
item.content:encoded:
Read the full article at https://simeononsecurity.com/

A separate Wi-Fi name does not reveal which devices communicate with each other. A mesh system might treat its guest network, IoT network, and wireless client isolation as different controls. This guide helps you test the paths on your own equipment without assuming a vendor’s label describes your policy.

Key Takeaways #

  • Prove the target works first: Reach a known service from your main network before testing a blocked path.
  • Test each boundary: Guest-to-main, IoT-to-main, and guest-to-guest access answer different questions.
  • Record the setup: Model, firmware, router or access-point mode, and connected mesh node affect interpretation.
  • Retest after changes: A clean result applies to the tested devices, service, address family, and configuration.

Before You Begin #

Allow about 20 minutes. You need a laptop able to join your main, guest, and IoT Wi-Fi networks. You also need a trusted device on the main network with a known open TCP service, such as a NAS web interface. A TCP service is a network service listening on a numbered port, such as a NAS web page on port 443. Use a service you own or administer. Note its local address and port without publishing them. Keep the service running throughout the test.

Write down the mesh model, firmware version, operating mode, and the settings for guest access, IoT access, shared devices, and client isolation. Confirm the laptop’s Wi-Fi name after every switch. Disconnect a VPN or proxy for this local-path test if your normal policy permits the change, then restore the VPN or proxy afterward. A VPN changes the route under test.

Warning: Test only your own devices or devices you have permission to administer. A router’s login page is a poor substitute for a main-network host because gateway access follows separate rules.

A local area network (LAN) is your private home network. Read More at https://simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: Why DNS Filtering Is Bypassed: Test the Resolver Path
item.description: Find why a device or browser skips your DNS filter. Compare direct and default queries, inspect logs, then check encrypted DNS, VPN, IPv6, and router settings.
item.content:encoded:
Read the full article at https://simeononsecurity.com/

You configured a filtering resolver, yet one device still reaches a domain your policy blocks. The cause might be the rule, the device’s Domain Name System (DNS) assignment, a browser’s encrypted resolver, or a VPN. Test the path before changing settings. A direct query to the filter and an ordinary device query answer different questions.

Key Takeaways #

  • Check the rule first: Confirm the filter receives and blocks a safe test domain.
  • Trace each layer: Router, operating system, browser, VPN, and mobile settings each influence DNS routing.
  • Use fresh queries: Match a new hostname and timestamp with the filter’s query log.
  • State the limit: One observed query proves one path, not every app or device.

Before You Begin #

Allow about 20 minutes. You need access to the filtering resolver’s query log, one device with the problem, and a record of the router’s DNS settings. Examples use a Windows laptop and Pi-hole, but the same comparison works with a resolver offering per-client query logs. Identify the exact filter address before starting. Do not paste private client addresses, query logs, or policy rules into a public report.

Choose a harmless test domain already blocked by your policy. Another option is a temporary exact deny rule for a domain you control in a test profile. Record the rule and remove the rule after testing. Do not use a live malware domain as a probe. A blocked page is a useful symptom, but the resolver log supplies the stronger path evidence.

item.title: 2x RTX 5060 Ti vs GB10: Five-Model Local AI Benchmark at 256K Context
item.description: A five-model RTX 5060 Ti versus GB10 comparison, plus a same-host Qwen3.8 Flash-Next Strata benchmark through 256K context.
item.content:encoded:
Read the full article at https://simeononsecurity.com/

Two RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB cards provide 32 GB of aggregate VRAM. An NVIDIA GB10 system provides 128 GB of coherent unified memory. The new five-model benchmark shows a more balanced result than the earlier Qwen-only test.

The dual-card system leads on generation speed for four of the five models at the 256K setting. The GB10 leads clearly on Qwen3.8 27B and keeps a larger memory reserve for models, context, and runtime allocations. The best choice depends on the model and workload.

A separate same-host run compared Qwen3.8-Flash-Next IQ2_XS on Strata with dense Qwen3.8 27B Q4_K_M on Ollama. The post-warmup generation median was 92.8 tokens per second for Flash-Next with a 260,446-token prompt. Dense Qwen3.8 reached 0.939 tokens per second with a 260,444-token prompt.

The NVIDIA GB10 uses 128 GB of coherent unified memory. NVIDIA lists the GB10 platform with 128 GB of LPDDR5x unified memory and a 140 W chip TDP. item.title: Build a Read-Only Active Directory Inventory With PowerShell
item.description: Inventory Active Directory OUs, users, and computers with scoped PowerShell queries. Export reviewable CSV files without changing directory objects.
item.content:encoded:
Read the full article at https://simeononsecurity.com/

An Active Directory cleanup starts with a trustworthy list of what exists. This read-only inventory gathers organizational units, users, and computers from one chosen scope. It exports three comma-separated values (CSV) files for review without changing directory objects. You still need to protect those files because names and device details reveal part of your environment.

Key Takeaways #

  • Choose a scope: Query one organizational unit before expanding to a whole domain.
  • Use read commands: Get-ADOrganizationalUnit, Get-ADUser, and Get-ADComputer retrieve objects.
  • Select fields: Export only the properties needed for the task.
  • Check the output: Compare counts and sample rows before relying on a report.

Before You Begin #

You need a Windows administration host with working DNS and network access to a domain controller, the ActiveDirectory PowerShell module, an account approved to read the selected objects, and a protected folder for CSV output. On a Windows client, the module comes from the Active Directory tools in Remote Server Administration Tools (RSAT). The site’s Active Directory module guide covers installation. Your capstone produces a deployment decision, not a running public service. Use your measured host and model data. Keep tests on loopback or an approved private lab network.

Choose a Track #

Beginner track: One user on one host. The runtime stays on loopback. The package proves model identity, acceptable task output, measured memory, local API access, and update rollback.

Advanced track: Several approved users on a private network. The runtime stays on loopback behind an authenticated TLS gateway. The package adds per-user authorization, rate limits, concurrency limits, monitoring, backup, staged updates, and access-denial evidence.

Your capstone is a security decision package for Patch Clerk. Another reviewer should reach the same deployment decision from your artifacts and evidence.

Scenario Change #

Patch Clerk now reads synthetic issues, reads repository files, proposes a patch, and applies a reviewed patch in a test repository. A product owner requests a new post_comment tool. The tool would publish text to a fictional issue system.

Your job is to decide whether post_comment enters the first release. Treat publication as an external side effect.
